children.name: Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment
children.blurb: Local and air-gapped model deployment covers running AI models on hardware the organization controls, from a workstation under a desk to a rack in a private data center, with no dependency on a public API.

children.name: Secure Storage and Networking for Legal Data
children.blurb: Secure storage and networking for legal data covers the systems and controls that hold and move client files, matter documents, privileged communications, contracts, discovery material, and case strategy.

children.name: Timekeeping and Billing Narratives
children.blurb: Timekeeping and billing narratives cover the written descriptions that lawyers and paralegals attach to billable time, along with the systems and rules that turn those entries into client invoices.

children.name: Firm Knowledge Management
children.blurb: Firm knowledge management covers the internal know-how a law firm creates and reuses, including precedents, clause banks, matter files, research memos, deal documents, and profiles of who knows what.

children.name: Client Intake and Triage
children.blurb: Client intake and triage covers the first structured contact between a prospective client and a legal team, including identity capture, conflict screening, matter description, urgency assessment, and routing to the right practice group.

sections.body: Legal operations, infrastructure and security is the part of AI in law that sits behind the desk rather than in front of a judge. It covers the machines, networks and workflows a firm needs before any model can touch client material: where the model runs, where the data lives, how work gets recorded and billed, how the firm's own knowledge is retrieved, and how new clients arrive. In practice, artificial intelligence here is doing summarization, classification, retrieval and first draft writing. A model reads an intake form and flags the practice area, or drafts a billing narrative from calendar and document activity. A retrieval system answers a question using the firm's own memos instead of the open web. None of this is autonomous legal reasoning, and the work is mostly about plumbing, permissions and evaluation.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some of this is genuinely solved. Retrieval over a firm's own documents works well when the corpus is clean and the questions are narrow, and transcription plus first pass summarization are reliable enough to save real time. What is not solved is the hard part: proving that a model never exposed privileged material, keeping an air-gapped deployment current without manual effort, and getting these tools to talk to practice management and billing systems that were never designed for them. Cost is unpredictable because usage based pricing meets unpredictable usage. Evaluation is thin, and most firms cannot say with confidence whether a change to a prompt or a model improved or degraded output. The regulatory backdrop keeps moving, and the site tracks 220 compliance and regulation pages for that reason, which is a measure of how much of this is still being written rather than settled.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section run from the foundation upward. Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment is where a reader starts if client data cannot leave the building, and it explains what running a model on firm hardware or an isolated network actually costs in capability and maintenance. Secure Storage and Networking for Legal Data sits directly beneath it, covering encryption, access control and network segmentation, the layer that decides whether the deployment is worth anything. Timekeeping and Billing Narratives is the output side, where models turn activity records into descriptions a client will accept. Firm Knowledge Management covers retrieval over the firm's own documents, the place where most of the practical value currently sits. Client Intake and Triage is the front door, where classification and routing decide what work the firm takes on and who handles it. Read together, they describe a stack rather than five separate tools.
